candidate.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — equity-focused perinatal quality improvement
candidate.educational_objective: When addressing inequities in maternal outcomes, evaluate clinical care quality together with access barriers, social and structural determinants of health, and potential bias rather than attributing outcomes primarily to individual patient behavior.

options.A: Examine quality-of-care processes, barriers to access, social and structural determinants of health, and potential bias when designing interventions.
options.B: Use patient education about individual health behaviors as the primary intervention and leave health-system factors outside the review.
options.C: Treat equal availability of the same written instructions as evidence that patients have equivalent access to high-quality care.
options.D: Exclude transportation, housing, and interpreter needs from the review because they are not clinical causes of maternal complications.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. CDC describes maternal-health inequities as multifactorial and identifies differences in quality of care, social determinants of health, access to care, social and structural determinants, stereotyping, and implicit bias as relevant considerations. CDC guidance for obstetric professionals specifically recommends assessing social and structural determinants, facilitating referrals for identified needs, ensuring interpreter access, recognizing stereotyping, and avoiding attribution of patient behavior solely to individual choices. B is incorrect because an equity review should not isolate individual behavior from health-system and structural factors. C is incorrect because identical written information does not establish equivalent access, communication, or quality of care. D is incorrect because CDC explicitly identifies transportation, housing, language access, and other social or structural factors as relevant to maternal health and health-care use.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Maternal-health inequities can reflect health-care quality, access, social and structural determinants, and bias; clinicians should assess these factors and avoid reducing patient behavior or outcomes to individual choice alone.
